items.why: The sentence sharply contrasts the five men entering and taking the objects with the priest and armed men standing outside.
The reader must distinguish the five men’s initial taking from the priest’s later taking of the same items.
“Our king” clearly refers to the trees, while gods and humans occur only in the vine’s earlier remark.
The passage explicitly links prosperity to the land lacking nothing, not to the comparison with Sidonians.
The stated reason is their missing inheritance; Israel’s lack of a king is only nearby background.
Jotham’s fear of Abimelek is explicit, while the citizens of Shechem enter the account later.
This tests the important distinction between the relatives carrying the message and the citizens receiving it.
It distinguishes the Levite’s purpose in leaving from Micah’s house, which he encounters only along the way.
The intended answer is a conditional wish rather than a clear request, making the stem unnatural.
“Does something” is too abstract and merely asks the reader to map “for him” back to the Levite.
It distinguishes the reported news that prompted the ambush from Abimelek’s later sight of people leaving the city.
The mother names her son as the intended maker, whereas the later action identifies the silversmith as the actual maker.
The pronoun resolves to Abimelek, but the final sentence gives his identity away and the competitor is implausible.
The occupants die from the deliberately set fire, though the alternative merely describes where they sought refuge.
It cleanly separates the priests’ service until captivity from the idol’s use while God’s house was at Shiloh.
The shouting immediately accompanies the Danites’ turn, though the prior overtaking makes the causal wording slightly debatable.
The fig tree’s rhetorical answer supplies its reason, while the move to the vine occurs only afterward.
The question distinguishes Abimelek’s specific purpose at the doorway from the broader attack already underway.
“Take it over” refers to the land, while the unsuspecting people are what the listeners will find there.
Micah explicitly bases his expectation on the Levite becoming his priest, not merely on the Levite’s origin.
The route distinction is answerable, but “the residence the Danites visit” makes the question needlessly awkward.
The pronoun follows Jerub-Baal and is confirmed by Jotham’s subsequent reference to “my father,” not Abimelek.
Zebul is the covert sender, whereas Gaal is the person whose statements provoke the message.
It tests the intermediary distinction: they address the priest so that he will inquire of God.
The curse largely restates the people’s punishment, and “after God punishes them” imposes an unclear sequence.
Zebul directly reinterprets the supposed people as mountain shadows, creating a clear perception contrast.
The result is stated in the “so that” clause, though the stem is stiff and the alternative belongs to the ensuing parable.
The olive tree explicitly frames giving up its honored oil as the cost of ruling; the fig tree appears only afterward.
Micah reports hearing the curse, but his wording clearly identifies his mother as its speaker.
It requires separating the later festival meal, when they curse Abimelek, from the earlier grape work.
The passage gives isolation and lack of relationships as the reason no rescuer comes, not the manner of attack.
